name: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty

clinicalPearls: The commonest cause of delayed puberty, representing an extreme of the normal timing spectrum rather than a disease, and much more frequently recognised in boys
Children are typically short for their age with a slow prepubertal growth velocity, but their height is appropriate for their delayed bone age
A family history of delayed puberty in a parent or sibling (late menarche in the mother, late growth spurt in the father) is characteristic
Bone age is delayed relative to chronological age, and predicted adult height based on bone age is usually within the mid-parental target range
It is fundamentally a diagnosis of exclusion, requiring confidence that permanent hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and chronic systemic illness have been ruled out
Reassurance and monitoring are often sufficient, since spontaneous puberty and a normal growth spurt eventually occur
When delay causes significant psychological distress, a short, low-dose course of sex steroids can be used to prime puberty and accelerate growth without compromising final height
reference.pathophysiology: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty represents a benign, self-limited lag in maturation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, so the reawakening of pulsatile GnRH secretion and the pubertal growth spurt occur later than average but ultimately proceed normally. Skeletal maturation is correspondingly delayed, meaning bone age lags behind chronological age but remains concordant with the child's height, which preserves growth potential and normal adult stature. The tendency is strongly familial. The principal clinical challenge is that the biochemical picture of low gonadotropins and sex steroids is shared with permanent hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, from which it can be difficult to distinguish before puberty finally begins.
additionalDifferentials: Permanent hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, including isolated GnRH deficiency and Kallmann syndrome
Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (e.g. Turner or Klinefelter syndrome, gonadal failure)
Chronic systemic illness (inflammatory bowel disease, coeliac disease, chronic kidney disease)
Undernutrition, eating disorders, or excessive exercise
Growth hormone deficiency or other pituitary hormone deficiencies
additionalInvestigations: Bone-age radiograph, which is delayed and central to the assessment
Basal LH, FSH, and sex-steroid measurement (low, consistent with prepubertal state)
Screening for chronic disease (full blood count, inflammatory markers, coeliac serology, renal and liver function)
Growth-velocity monitoring plotted serially on a growth chart
Karyotype where a chromosomal cause of hypogonadism is suspected
redFlags: Anosmia or hyposmia, midline defects, or cryptorchidism/micropenis suggesting congenital GnRH deficiency rather than simple delay
Features of a chronic systemic illness or malnutrition underlying the delay
Neurological symptoms or visual field defects suggesting an intracranial or pituitary lesion
Failure of any pubertal progression by the upper age limits despite an appropriate period of observation
reference.prognosis: Excellent, with spontaneous onset of puberty and a normal growth spurt leading to an adult height within the genetic target range; the main morbidity is psychosocial, arising from the discrepancy with peers during the waiting period.
pitfalls: Labelling delay as constitutional without adequately excluding permanent hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, which cannot always be distinguished before puberty starts
Missing an underlying chronic illness or nutritional disorder presenting as pubertal delay
Interpreting short stature as pathological without accounting for the delayed bone age
Overlooking the psychological impact and withholding a reasonable short course of priming therapy
Failing to arrange follow-up to confirm that puberty eventually progresses
management: Offer reassurance and expectant monitoring as first-line management, since spontaneous puberty and a normal growth spurt reliably follow
Consider a short course of low-dose sex-steroid therapy — testosterone in boys, oestrogen in girls — to initiate pubertal development and relieve psychosocial distress where waiting is difficult
Track growth velocity serially on a growth chart alongside bone-age radiographs
Exclude chronic systemic illness and permanent hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, as this remains a diagnosis of exclusion
Provide psychosocial support for the distress arising from the discrepancy with peers
Re-evaluate for permanent hypogonadotropic hypogonadism if puberty fails to begin spontaneously within the expected window
